title: Quarantine Policy
description:
Per-artifact overrides of how quarantine issues are handled.

The configuration's 'problem-policy' table says what the rules are, for every artifact a run touches.  This file says which specific artifacts are exceptions to them, and why.  Keeping the two apart is deliberate: an exception is reviewable on its own in a pull request, it carries a justification, and it is edited on a completely different cadence from the configuration around it.

It overrides in both directions.  Loosening is the common case - 'this one is a false positive' - but an entry may name any of the four classes, so tightening a single artifact is as expressible as excusing one.

rules.title: Artifact Overrides
rules.description: Checked in order; the first rule matching both the artifact and the code wins.  Order therefore matters, and a narrow rule belongs above a broad one.

purl.description: Which artifact, as a purl.  A version qualifier is a RANGE in the artifact's own ecosystem, not a glob: 'pkg:npm/tuna@<2' means every npm version below 2 by npm's ordering, which a textual match cannot express.  A purl naming no version matches every version.

codes.description:
Which problem codes this rule answers.  Required, and there is deliberately no way to say 'every code for this artifact': excusing a missing signature should not thereby excuse a malware finding on the same artifact.

The list is every code that says something about an artifact - a wider question than 'is this a classic quarantine'.  'dependency-unresolved' and 'pom-property-unresolved' are nobody's idea of quarantine and are still things you may want to state a handling for on one package.  It is the same list the configuration's 'problem-policy' table accepts, because a code you can set a rule for run-wide is exactly one you can make an exception to here.

Absent are the codes that are not about an artifact.  Faults in the input a run was given - 'config-invalid', 'config-unreadable', 'file-unreadable', 'lock-format-unknown', 'lock-unrecognized', 'lock-malformed', 'enumeration-unsupported', 'sample-percent-unsupported' - are fail-fast and deliberately beyond the reach of configuration: a rule that could excuse an unreadable lock file would be excusing the file that names the artifacts.  And the tool's own state - 'unimplemented', 'aborted' - has nothing an artifact could be an exception to.

class.description: How these codes are handled for this artifact.

justification.description: Why this exception is acceptable.  Not required by the schema, and strongly worth writing: an exception nobody can re-evaluate is one nobody will ever dare remove.

expires.title: Expiry
expires.description:
When this override lapses: an RFC 3339 timestamp, or the word 'never'.

Required, and 'never' has to be written out.  An acknowledgement with no end date should be a decision somebody made and wrote down, not what happens when a field is left out - and one field with two spellings beats two fields that can contradict each other.

After the date, the artifact falls back to the problem-policy default.  validate-config reports overrides that have already lapsed, so a list of exceptions can be pruned rather than accumulating until nobody dares delete one.
